How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Passive ambient audio sampling bears great potential for objectively measuring daily social activity and its association with wellbeing and health. However, detecting true conversations via human annotation is labor-intensive, and automatic labeling via audio signal processing has thus far only received proof-of-concept validation. Here, we conduct a comprehensive psychometric validation of a deep learning-based foreground speech detection algorithm for conversation activity detection (CAD) from ambient audio sampled with the Electronically Activated Recorder (EAR) method (Hebbar et al., 2021). We assess the CAD algorithm's validity as an objective measure of conversation activity using four archival EAR datasets with human groundtruth conversation annotations (N = 561 participants, n = 167,539 audio recordings). Specifically, we evaluate, across the four samples, the degree to which the CAD algorithm converges with human-annotated conversation activity, yields temporal stability estimates of conversation activity, and replicates patterns of external correlates (with demographic, wellbeing, and personality measures) comparable to those derived from human ground-truth annotations. We further compare the distributional properties of conversation activity derived from the CAD algorithm and human ground-truth annotations. Overall, the CAD algorithm evidences strong psychometric properties for estimating conversation activity across a range of participants and study characteristics, suggesting that it is suitable for at-scale deployment to objectively measure daily socializing from passively sampled ambient audio.

Psychometric Validation of a Deep Learning-based Foreground Speech Detection Algorithm for Everyday Conversation Detection

In a world of pervasive social technologies, humans are, paradoxically, feeling increasingly lonely and spending less time with others than in the past. A lack of meaningful social connection is consistently linked to negative mental and physical health outcomes, including increased risks of depression, dementia, cardiovascular disease, and even mortality (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2015; Office of Surgeon General, 2023). The impact of these effects appears to be comparable to the effects of other negative health behaviors, including cigarette smoking, consuming alcohol, and physical inactivity (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2017). Yet, while guidelines set by national health organizations feature standards for these and other physical health behaviors, they fail to provide them for social health behaviors. Before recommendations can be made regarding socializing and physical and mental health, though, reliable, accurate, efficient, objective, and ideally passive measures of everyday socializing must first be developed. An important starting point is refining our understanding of individuals' everyday social interactions.

Historically, researchers have relied on self-report surveys to measure social interactions.

The Social Network Index (Berkman & Syme, 1979) asks questions like "How many friends do you see at least once a month?" and the Social Isolation Scale features items related to social activities, such as "How often do you get together with people you have met in your neighborhood?" (Greenfield et al., 2002). The American Time Use Survey (ATUS) asks interviewees to recall and report their social interactions from 4 am the day prior to 4 am the day of the interview (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). While these self-report measures are efficient to implement at scale, they are less than ideal for measuring social interactions because of limitations in what participants can accurately report. Even with best intentions, when participants report on a specific time period (e.g., a day), they are unlikely to remember every instance of a behavior, particularly when it is very short and seemingly trivial (Boswell et al., 2020; Schwarz, 2012). Yet, as research has shown, even fleeting social interactions are consequential for social connection and support (e.g., Moreton et al., 2023; Ascigil et al., 2025) but are unlikely to be consistently recalled and reported.

Ambulatory assessment methods are the gold-standard for addressing key limitations of self-report surveys, such as memory-related reporting biases (Löchner et al., 2025). Although still reliant on an individual's first-person account, self-report-based ambulatory assessment methods allow capturing experiences and behaviors in situ, that is within the flow of daily life, and in vivo, that is (close to) real-time (Myin-Germeys & Kuppens, 2022). Depending on the sampling approach, participants are asked to report on their social interactions over a period of time (e.g., the past hour, Sun et al., 2020; Kroencke et al., 2023) or are expected to complete a survey every time a social interaction occurs (e.g., "every interaction of 10 minutes or more, no matter how routine or seemingly pointless" (p. 744, the Rochester Interaction Record, Wheeler & Nezlek, 1977). Recall bias is reduced as the time window between social interaction and assessment is minimized (Boswell et al., 2020).

However, the demands of ambulatory assessment, such as repeated in-the-moment assessments that create interruptions in the flow of the day, can create a non-trivial burden for participants. To address this, researchers often limit their sampling frequency (e.g., to few daily prompts or few assessment days) to prevent potential loss of data quality (e.g., attrition, missing data, careless responding, Fritz et al., 2025; Wrzus & Neubauer, 2023). Event-contingent sampling further requires participants to continuously monitor whether the critical to-be-assessed event has happened. In the case of social interactions, this means having to constantly take a "step back" to monitor whether one is engaged in a social interaction and whether it is exceeding 10 minutes. This self-monitoring process can induce psychological processes such as selfawareness and evaluation apprehension that, in turn, can influence the "object of measurement," social interaction.

As an alternative (or complement) to these self-report approaches, researchers have increasingly turned to observational ambulatory assessment methods to capture everyday social behavior more objectively, such as wearable cameras (Brown et al., 2017) and ambient audio sampling (Demiray et al., 2020). The Electronically Activated Recorder (EAR), for instance, samples snippets of ambient audio around a person intermittently throughout the day (Mehl, 2017). The EAR is an (acoustic) observational ambulatory assessment method for capturing social interactions in a broad range of studies with both healthy (college students, Macbeth et al., 2022; hockey youth athletes, Sutcliffe et al., 2021; cognitively normal adults, Polsinelli et al., 2020) and clinical populations (individuals with schizophrenia-spectrum personality disorders, Minor et al., 2018; patients with breast cancer; Robbins et al., 2011 Robbins et al., , 2014)). Since its inception 25+ years ago, it has emerged as a generally well-accepted method with overall good reliability and validity for assessing daily social interactions (Mehl & Pennebaker, 2003; Mehl & Holleran, 2007; Mehl, 2017).

The EAR method can navigate several challenges associated with self-report measures.

First, it requires minimal active participant effort, with the only requirement being wearing the device. Previous studies have reported high compliance (Manson & Robbins, 2017). Second, the EAR operates relatively unobtrusively as participants adjust to wearing the device thus limiting its influence on their behaviors (or their thoughts of how they should behave; Mehl & Holleran, 2007). On the other hand, the EAR comes with its own limitations. While procedures are in place to ensure EAR data privacy and confidentiality, there are ethical and legal implications around recording raw audio that can contain sensitive information about the participant as well as potentially third parties, such as bystanders who are not enrolled in the study (Mehl, 2017). Furthermore, and of great practical importance for researchers wanting to implement the EAR method into their research, the "manual" (i.e. human-based) processing of EAR data tends to be very labor intensive. Research assistants must undergo extensive training and calibration, and the listening to and annotating of the sound files is extremely time-consuming (Kaplan et al., 2020), which has limited its potential as a method due to its extensive and lengthy data processing.

Towards Automatic Conversation Activity Detection

Engineering and computer scientists have been exploring the potential of audio signal processing for more efficiently detecting conversation activity. One of the first methods to automatically extract conversation activity from ambient audio was the BeWell app (Lane et al., 2011). The BeWell app was designed to monitor and provide real-time feedback to users on their levels of social interactions (as well as their sleep and physical activity). It measured social isolation based on the total duration of ambient voices captured via the built-in smartphone microphone (Lane et al., 2014). While BeWell achieved 85% accuracy for detecting social interactions in a proof-of-concept study, the validation was comprised of very few participants (five users; Lane et al., 2011). An additional study with three other users further found that the BeWell app overestimated social interactions by about 14%, likely due to misclassifying nonconversational voices (e.g., from the TV) as instances of conversations (Lane et al., 2011).

The BeWell application later evolved into the StudentLife application (Wang et al., 2014). Continuing to measure both physical activity and sleep, StudentLife, in this case, measured both the frequency and duration of social interactions based on the ambient voices picked up by the smartphone microphone. Specifically, it uses voice activity detection to monitor speech in a person's stream of ambient audio and identifies conversation duration via the on-and off-set detection of speech activity. The StudentLife application was initially used with undergraduate students but has since been widely employed with other populations (e.g., Wang et al., 2020), with its voice classifier emerging as one of the most widely used for conversation activity detection (Harari & Gosling, 2023). Having revealed many important links between the objective social sensor data and mental health, the underlying question about the voice classifier's specificity remains. The same classifier has recently been implemented in the opensource AWARE Conversations plugin (Ferreira & Mulukutla, 2020), which continues to be widely used in the field, often along with a caveat that the classifier might be prone to false positives in certain daily-life contexts (Harari et al., 2020; Krämer et al., 2023; Roos et al., 2023; Wrzus et al., 2025).

Taken together, combining the EAR's unobtrusive observation approach to capturing social interactions within the ambient noise of everyday life with a conversation activity detection algorithm may help address limitations of traditional voice activity detection algorithms in reliably identifying actual conversations at scale.

The Present Study

The present project pursues a construct validation of a deep-learning-based foreground speech detection algorithm for everyday conversation activity detection (CAD) within the paradigm of the EAR method (Hebbar et al., 2021). Adapting a speaker-agnostic foreground speech detection algorithm from the field of audio signal processing (Nadarajan et al., 2019) to the context of sampled ambient sounds, the CAD algorithm address challenges found in uncontrolled ambient audio (e.g., background speech, TV/radio speech) and localizes foreground speech to estimate the probability that an EAR sound file contains conversation activity. The algorithm is speaker-agnostic, that is, it does not require being trained on "knowing" the primary speaker's voice and is therefore sensitive to (different) voices in the acoustic foreground (Hebbar et al., 2021). The algorithm was developed (i.e. trained and evaluated) using two archival EAR datasets (215 participants; 89,454 sound files) for which full human conversation annotations were available (O'Hara et al., 2020; Polsinelli et al., 2020). The CAD algorithm achieved high precision and recall, demonstrating good classification performance (AUCs = .87) across both EAR samples (Hebbar et al., 2021), and, importantly, achieved good suppression of false positive (i.e. voice but not conversation) predictions. The CAD algorithm therefore has the potential to serve as a suitable tool for measuring everyday conversation activity from EAR-sampled ambient audio.

Recently, the field has repeatedly called for extending algorithm developments beyond basic tests of prediction accuracy into the classical domain of measurement and psychometric validation (Bleidorn & Hopwood, 2019; Harari & Gosling, 2023; Stachl et al., 2020; Tay et al., 2020). While basic prediction accuracy validations are useful for establishing feasibility, systematic evaluations of an algorithm's psychometric properties are needed if the algorithm is to be used for real-stake psychological measurement and clinical intervention. The current project therefore sought to subject the CAD algorithm (Hebbar et al., 2021) to a systematic psychometric validation to evaluate its potential to serve as a measure of the quantity of daily conversation activity. We evaluate the CAD algorithms' construct validity by utilizing four archival EAR datasets that feature full human ground-truth in-conversation annotations. Specifically, we investigate the following five research questions around the CAD algorithms' construct validity:

Methods

The study combined data from N = 561 participants across four samples that range in study contexts and participant characteristics. All samples from which the data originated had IRB approval. Descriptions of each sample and its measures are outlined below. A summary of sample characteristics and EAR features is presented in Table 1. 2012-2013 2007-2011 2007-2011 2010-2013 2015-2019 EAR Version iEAR PocketEAR PocketEAR PocketEAR; iEAR Android EAR Sampling rate 30s every 12.5 mins 50s every 9 mins 50s every 9 mins 30s every 12 mins or 50s every 9 mins 30s every 24 mins # of days EAR was worn 9 days (3 weekends) 3 days (1 weekend) 3 days (1 weekend) 6 days (2 weekends) 21 days (3 weeks) # of valid waking sound files 44,691 7,176 7,268 50,762 57,642 # of all sound files 62,523 10,245 10,680 76,949 74,411

Participants and Procedures

Sample 1 (Divorce Study)

Data were utilized from 122 recently separated or divorced adults (M age = 44.1 years, SD age = 10.5 years, 71.3% female, 62.8% White/Non-Hispanic) recruited from the Tucson, Arizona area. The study involved five monthly visits during which participants completed selfreport measures about their life satisfaction and depression. Personality traits were measured at the initial visit. The EAR was worn for 3 consecutive days (Friday through Sunday) every other visit (i.e., every 2 months, n = 44,691 audio recordings). Further information about this study is reported in O'Hara et al. (2020). This sample was part of the original CAD algorithm development study as part of the training data (Hebbar et al., 2021).

Samples 2a and 2b (Breast Cancer Study)

Data were originally collected from 52 breast cancer patients and their partners who were recruited from the Arizona Cancer Center in Tucson, Arizona. Due to discrepancies in file name structure when integrating the ground-truth data with the algorithm data, only data from fortyfour female breast cancer patients ( M age = 55.0 years, SD age = 14.0 years, 79.6% White) and their partners ( M age = 57.4 years, SD age = 14.1 years, 81.8% male, 77.3% White) were usable for the current analysis. Life satisfaction and depression were measured at baseline and at 3-month follow-up. Personality traits were measured at baseline. The EAR was worn for 3 consecutive days (Friday through Sunday; breast cancer patients: n = 7,176 audio recordings; partners: n = 7,268). Further information about this sample is reported in Robbins et al. (2014).

Sample 3 (Meditation Study)

Data were originally collected from 208 healthy adults who were recruited from the Atlanta, Georgia area for a randomized control trial of an 8-week meditation intervention. Due to mislabeling of audio files for a specific participant, only data from 207 healthy adults ( M age = 33.6 years, SD age = 8.3 years, 65.2% female, 50.2% White) were usable for the current analysis.

Participants completed self-report measures about their life satisfaction, depression, and extraversion pre-and post-intervention. The EAR was also worn pre-and post-intervention for 3 consecutive days each (Friday through Sunday; n = 50,762 audio recordings). Further information about this sample is reported in Kaplan et al. (2022).

Sample 4 (Suicidality Study)

Data were utilized from 144 adolescents ( M age = 15.1 years, SD age = 1.5 years, 69.4% female, 76.1% White) who were hospitalized for suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STB). The study consisted of 3 weeks of ambulatory assessment during which the EAR was worn (n = 57,642 audio recordings). Depression was measured at baseline and following the 3-week assessment. Further information about this sample is reported in Nugent et al. (2022).

Measures

Life Satisfaction

Participants from samples 1 through 3 completed the 5-item Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS; Diener et al., 1985). Items included, "In most ways my life is close to my ideal" and "So far I have gotten the important things I want in life" and were answered from a scale of 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). Items were averaged to reflect an individual's global life satisfaction. Internal consistencies, calculated as Cronbach's alpha ranged from .84 to .92.

Depression

Participants from samples 2 and 4 completed the 20-item Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D; Radloff, 1977). Participants from sample 1 completed the shortened 10-item version (CESD-R-10; Andresen et al., 1994). Both versions included items such as, "I was bothered by things that usually don't bother me" and "I felt everything I did was an effort" and were answered from a scale of 0 (Rarely or none of the time) to 3 (Most or all of the time). Participants from sample 3 completed the 21-item Beck Depression Inventory (BDI, Beck et al., 1996) on a 4-point scale (0 to 3). In all samples, items were summed up to reflect an individual's level of depressive symptoms. Cronbach's alphas ranged from .83 to .94.

Personality Traits

Participants from samples 1 through 3 reported their personality traits using the 44-item Big Five Inventory (BFI; John et al., 1991). Items included, "is talkative" and "worries a lot" and were answered from a scale of 1 (Disagree strongly) to 7 (Agree strongly). Items for each subscale were averaged to reflect an individual's level of a specific personality trait. Cronbach's alphas for extraversion, conscientiousness, openness to experience, agreeableness, and neuroticism ranged from .71 to .89.

Ground-truth 'In Conversation' Annotations

In all samples, participants wore the EAR, typically from the time they woke up to the time they went to bed. Across studies, the number of days the EAR was worn and the sampling rate varied, with the EAR generally sampling between 5 and 10% of participants' waking hours per day. For every audio recording, trained research assistants coded for a range of aspects of an individual's social life (as acoustically captured), including whether the participant was engaged in a conversation. The coders were instructed to code the participant as engaged in a conversation if the participant spoke at least one word (or a verbal backchannel) during the audio recording (Mehl & Pennebaker, 2003). Therefore, the codings capture the participant in a state of conversation rather than actively talking (i.e. the participant could be listening for most of the sound file). Also, the codings capture specifically spoken conversations, so conversations with other people who are physically present or conversations over the phone, rather than digitalmediated interactions over text messaging or social media.

For samples 1-3, two trained coders independently coded all audio recordings for a given participant. For sample 4, about half of the sample was coded by two trained coders and the other half by one. For all samples, the coders also identified audio recordings where participants appeared to be sleeping and/or non-compliant (i.e. not wearing the EAR). To obtain a more accurate estimate of the prevalence of conversations (and a more accurate test of how well the CAD estimates the prevalence of conversations), these audio recordings were subsequently excluded. The remaining files were aggregated at the participant level, to reflect the portion of participants' valid (i.e. adhering to wearing the EAR) waking (i.e. non-sleeping) sound files where they were engaged in spoken conversations.

Conversation Activity Detection Algorithm

The CAD is a deep-learning-based foreground speech detection algorithm that has been specifically developed (i.e. fine-tuned; cf. Nadarajan et al., 2019) for the detection of conversation activity from everyday ambient audio recorded with the EAR method (Hebbar et al., 2021). As part of the algorithm development, its accuracy was tested on two archival EAR data sets (one overlapping with data included here, Sample 1), yielding Area Under the Curve accuracy estimates of .87 for the best-performing model (SAD embeddings), which is the version we employed and evaluated here.

For each sample, all audio files recorded by the EAR within the study were processed by the CAD algorithm. For each file, the CAD algorithm provided a posterior probability value between 0 to 1. To obtain a conversation activity estimate that is commensurate to the one for the human ground-truth annotations, only the posterior probability values of files that ground-truth coders deemed valid (i.e. adhering to wearing the EAR) and waking (i.e. not sleeping) were used.

The resulting variable based on valid, waking sound files is indexed as CAD VA . In addition, we computed a conversation activity index based on all recorded files, including the files where the participant was deemed non-compliant and asleep. To the CAD algorithm's practical utility, it is also important to evaluate how well it performs with data that were not "pre-reviewed" by a human annotator. Although the CAD algorithm likely involves a loss of validity when deployed to all recordings irrespective of whether the ambient sounds actually "belonged" to the participant (i.e. the participant was or was not awake and wearing the EAR), this information might not be available when the CAD is proactively employed on new EAR data, rather than retroactively on pre-processed archival data. The resulting variable based on all recorded sound files is indexed as CAD ALL . For both variables, the posterior probability values were averaged at the participant level as estimates of participants' conversation activity.

Transparency and Openness

The study's design and analyses reported in this paper were not preregistered. Data and code for reproducing reported results for all samples are available on the Open Science Framework (OSF): https://osf.io/rta8u/overview?view_only=c1a3f6ee676e46a9a667a25d70ace795

https://osf.io/rta8u/overview?view_only=c1a3f6ee676e46a9a667a25d70ace795. The audio recordings from which the analyzed variables are derived cannot be made available to protect participants' privacy. The algorithm, accompanying installation instructions, and sample recordings are also available, using the link provided above. Consent has been obtained from all individuals included in the sample recordings. All analyses were conducted using R Statistical Software Version 4.4.0 (R Core Team, 2024).

Analytic Strategy

Bivariate Pearson correlations were run at the participant level. We examined the association between the ground-truth (indexed as GT) and the CAD estimates as a measure of convergent validity. To assess the degree to which the CAD and GT estimates yielded comparable temporal stability estimates, we transformed the correlation coefficients of the GT and the CAD estimates at different time points into Fisher's z values (to correct for skewness resulting from correlations' bounded nature). The Fisher's z values were then averaged and backtransformed into correlation coefficients to obtain a single estimate of test-retest reliability/temporal stability. To assess the degree to which the CAD and GT estimates yielded comparable external correlates, we correlated both with the respective variables of interest. To account for differences in scales used across samples, we converted the units of our external criteria (e.g., life satisfaction, depression, personality) to Percentage of Maximum Possible (POMP; Cohen et al., 1999) scores. In doing so, a zero on a given measure reflects the minimum possible score while a 100 reflects the maximum possible score. Descriptive statistics of the external criteria are presented in Table 2. Further, to evaluate the degree of correspondence between the sets of correlations obtained from the CAD estimates and the GT estimates, we calculated profile or column-vector correlations. Comparing external correlates and reviewing the profile correlations allows us to evaluate the extent the CAD preserves the pattern of associations with empirically relevant variables. Finally, to assess the degree to which the CAD and the GT have overlapping (or unique) predictive validity, we fitted multiple linear regressions for each external criterion with the CAD and GT variables entered simultaneously as predictors and assessed the resulting semi-partial correlations. The rationale underlying these analyses is that, ideally, the CAD estimates share maximum variance with the corresponding GT estimates, and the GT estimates fail to predict unique variance in the presence of the CAD estimates (in other words, ideally, the CAD captures "everything GT captures"). Conversely, unless the CAD estimate "sees" something that the GT does not, the CAD estimates should fail to predict unique variance in the presence of the GT estimates. Finally, to compare the distributional properties of the CAD and GT estimates, kernel density plots were generated for each sample and descriptive statistics (e.g., means, standard deviations) were computed and compared.

For all analyses, we evaluated the magnitude of correlation differences between the CAD and the GT by adapting effect size interpretation guidelines suggested by Funder and Ozer (2019). More specifically, we considered CAD-GT correlation coefficient differences from |.00| Note. M and SD are used to represent the standardized (i.e., POMP-scored) mean and standard deviation, respectively. For samples where more than one assessment was available, the minimum alpha value is reported.

Results

RQ 1: To What Degree do the CAD Algorithm's Estimates of Conversation Activity Converge with the Human-annotated GT Estimates?

We correlated the CAD algorithm's estimates of conversation activity with the humanannotated GT estimates to evaluate overall convergent validity. Table 3 shows the correlations for each sample. Across the four datasets, CAD and GT estimates converged moderately to strongly, with correlations for CAD VA ranging from .475 to .873. Although the correlations were high for Sample 1, which was included in the training data, the strongest correlations arose for Sample 2, "unseen" data and the oldest data, collected between 2005 and 2009 with a technologically basic Windows Mobile based Pocket PC Personal Digital Assistant. Sample 4 differed from the other samples in that the participants were adolescents, rather than adults. Consistent with this, and the associated difference in social environments, convergence was lower but still substantial (.590).

As expected, the convergence correlations were generally lower for CAD ALL , ranging from .390 to .779 (apart from Sample 4). However, interestingly, the estimates based on all available sound files resulted in minimal effect size differences (r diff ≤ |.10|; with the exception of Sample 2b: r diff = .187 ) from those where the participant was deemed (by a human coder) awake and wearing the EAR.

RQ 2: To What Degree do the CAD Algorithm and the GT Annotations Yield Comparable Temporal Stability Estimates of Conversation Activity?

For samples where more than one EAR measurement occasion was available (all samples other than Sample 2), we calculated temporal stability estimates of conversation activity for the CAD and GT. Temporal stability indicates the extent the conversation activity estimates provided by both CAD and GT were consistent across time. Both CAD and GT estimates showed substantial stability across all three samples. Interestingly, the CAD stability estimates were slightly higher than the GT ones, although the effect size differences were minimal (other than for CAD ALL in Sample 3). CAD VA and CAD ALL yielded largely comparable stability estimates and, despite the lower Sample 3 overall CAD-GT convergence, the resulting temporary stability estimates were highly comparable to the other samples. Table 4 shows the estimates for each sample.

RQ 3: To What Degree do the CAD and the GT Estimates of Conversation Activity Yield Comparable Relationships with External Criteria?

The correlations of the CAD and GT estimates with the external criteria are presented in

Table 5. Across the four samples, nine external measures (i.e. demographics, wellbeing, and personality), and two CAD estimates ( CAD VA and CAD ALL ), only minimal (|.00| ≤ |.10|; 58 out of 74 correlations, 78%) to small (|.10| ≤ |.20|; 16 out of 74 correlations, 22%) effect size differences emerged, suggesting that the CAD emulated the GT effects overall with high precision.

Sample 1, which was part of the training data, exhibited the smallest average effect size differences ( CAD VA = .034, CAD ALL = .031), but not much higher ones emerged for the unseen data in the other three samples. Only the CAD ALL estimate in Sample 2b (.103) and both CAD estimates in Sample 3 ( CAD VA = .080, CAD ALL = .083) yielded slightly higher average effect size differences. Despite the differences in participant characteristics and, by extension, social environments in Sample 4, the CAD emulated the GT effects there with high precision (average average r diff for CAD VA = .059 ; average r diff for CAD ALL = .068 ).

Profile correlations between the arrays of correlations obtained for the CAD and GT estimates also support the picture of the CAD's overall high precision, in this case in form of a comparable tracking of the relative patterning of the correlations. Very strong profile correlations emerged for Sample 1, 2a, and 2b (range: .933 to .976 for CAD VA and .854 to .983 for CAD ALL ), again with slightly lower ones for Sample 3 ( CAD VA = .664, CAD ALL = .631). No profile correlations were computed for Sample 4 due to the small number of variables.

RQ 4: To What Degree do the CAD and GT Estimates of Conversation Activity have Overlapping (or Unique) Validity for Predicting External Criteria?

Table 6 presents the squared semi-partial correlations from a multiple regression predicting the external criteria simultaneously from both the CAD and GT estimates. Ideally, the CAD and GT estimates would be highly redundant with neither uniquely predicting variance above and beyond the other. To the extent that GT is a "better" measure, it should emerge as a unique predictor; and, if the CAD were to emerge as a unique predictor, it would point to the CAD capturing (somehow) aspects of conversation activity that GT "misses".

Across the four samples and nine external measures, very few statistically significant squared semi-partial correlations emerged for GT controlling for CAD (7 out of 148 correlations, 4.73%; sr 2 s = |.00| ≤ |.05|). This suggests that the CAD estimates by and large "absorbed" the predictive variance in the GT estimates.

RQ 5: How do the Distributional Properties of the CAD and GT Estimates Compare?

To evaluate the extent to which the CAD and GT estimates produce comparable distributions, we visualized them via kernel density plots and calculated descriptive statistics (M, SD) for each sample. As depicted in Figure 1a-e, the CAD estimates, i.e. the algorithm's posterior probabilities as measures of proportion of time in conversation, consistently underestimates conversation activity. This is least the case in Sample 1, which was part of the training data, but the underestimation is quite pronounced for the other samples, particularly for Sample 4 which differs most in participant characteristics and, by extension, social environments. The CAD also results in reduced variance relative to GT. The underestimation and the variance reduction is slightly more pronounced for the CAD ALL estimates than the CAD VA estimates. Interestingly and importantly, though, the CAD estimates' restricted range does not appear to undermine its convergent validity and psychometric precision as evaluated in RQ 1 through 4, suggesting that the CAD's raw posterior probabilities are psychometrically well suited for reproducing rank-orders and between-person variability in relative terms. Distributions and Descriptive Statistics for Each Sample

Discussion

This study reports the results of a comprehensive psychometric validation of a deep learning-based foreground speech detection algorithm for conversation activity detection from ambient audio sampled with the EAR method. Overall, the CAD algorithm demonstrated sound construct validity as an objective measure of conversation activity. Across four participant and context diverse EAR data sets (with a total sample size of 561 participants, ranging from 13 to 85 years of age), the CAD and GT estimates converged moderately to strongly. The CAD and GT estimates also resulted in comparable temporal stability estimates and showed overall comparable relationships with external criteria. The CAD and GT estimates captured similar variance in external criteria, with one rarely contributing additional predictive value for an outcome beyond the other. Further, the CAD algorithm's validity emerged as strong for estimates derived from only those sound files that were coded as valid and, with a small validity decrement, all sound files, irrespective of participants' deemed compliance and wakefulness.

As a tool for estimating conversation activity from ambient sounds, the CAD algorithm has several strengths that should be highlighted. In terms of its function, the CAD algorithm captures conversations that are localized in the foreground, building on previous traditional voice activity-based algorithms that have been subject to validity concerns around false positive classifications when used across the range of everyday situations which can feature complex and hard to classify ambient sound scenes (Harari et al., 2020; Krämer et al., 2023). Further, the algorithm is speaker-agnostic, meaning that the estimation of the presence of a conversation is not tied to a specific speaker, for example the participant's voice (Hebbar et al., 2021). While pinpointing participant speech (vs. conversation partner speech) may be an aim for future investigations (e.g., to estimate relative contributions to a conversation), we believe a speakeragnostic approach is inclusive of not only individual differences in conversation participation (e.g., being more of a listener rather than leading the conversation) but also allows the capturing of one aspect of audible social context for individuals who may be facing language or cognitive limitations (e.g., aphasic patients after a stroke, Dhand et al., 2026). At the same time, as ambient audio signal progressing capabilities expand, more complex approaches that, for example, consider and estimate turn-taking and relative contributions will allow estimating additional, important social connection parameters (Ahmed et al., 2026; Liang, Zhang, & Thomaz, 2023; Zhang et al., 2026).

The current investigation can help advance the development of comprehensive approaches for validating AI-algorithms for use in real-stakes psychological research and decision making, which has recently garnered considerable attention (Klus et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2024; Wright et al., 2026). From a computer and engineering science perspective, algorithm development has historically focused on accuracy in terms of correspondence to a ground-truth criterion. However, when psychologists want to use algorithm outputs as psychological measures, the field's measurement tradition argues in favor of full-scale psychometric validations. This is particularly the case when those algorithmic psychological measures are used for consequential (e.g., clinical) decision making. Following this standard, we evaluated the CAD algorithm's construct validity and generalizability. Testing it --and finding overall strong evidence of convergent validity and generalizability --across three quite heterogeneous unseen samples that span a range of data collection times (from 2005 to 2019), mobile devices (from Pocket PCs and iPod Touch devices to Android smartphones), and participant characteristics (from cancer patients and their partners to adolescents after a hospitalization for suicidal ideation) can provide confidence regarding its suitability for at-scale deployment to objectively measure daily socializing from passively sampled ambient audio.

variability than GT. While this creates challenges for research questions where absolute values are of interest (e.g., the percentage of time people spend in conversation; Pfeifer & Mehl, 2026), the CAD algorithm's estimates based on these posterior probabilities can be expected to have sound validity for research questions that investigate covariation between conversation activity and other variables (e.g., correlation/ regression research). For instance, the CAD may be helpful in identifying patients who exhibit lower conversation activity than others, as a behavioral indicator alongside self-reported symptoms for clinicians to consider as they determine whether assessment or support is warranted. Future research can also consider the deployment of the CAD algorithm to a broader range of archival EAR samples (e.g., Tidwell et al., 2025) to identify optimal conversation activity detection thresholds (based on population and life context characteristics) and their validity implications.

Finally, we find the decision between CAD VA and CAD ALL to be another important point of consideration. Indeed, although we believe that CAD VA provides, at the conceptual level, a cleaner estimation of conversation quantity, it does practically still require some basic manual coding of each sound file, which can quickly get immensely time consuming (Kaplan et al., 2020). Arguably, if a researcher is in the position to allocate sufficient human resources to determine for each sound file in a study whether the participant was awake and wearing the EAR, it would effectively add very little time to also have the human coders determine whether a sound file contained a conversation (i.e. the ground truth). In that sense, our findings regarding the (overall good) validity of the CAD ALL estimates may practically constitute the most important information. If a researcher can tolerate the (slight) validity decrement that comes with deploying the CAD algorithm to all of a project's sound files, the time and resources savings are potentially immense, considering that obtaining the ground-truth codings for the samples included here took each several years. A practical recommendation to maximize the validity of the CAD ALL estimates is to tailor the EAR sampling times closely to individual participants' expected waking hours.

Constraints on Generality

Our sample consisted of individuals primarily from the southern United States. Further, majority of the participants identified as White and female. Lastly, there is limited representation of those in older adulthood (65+ years of age). The data also primarily came from English speakers. Thus, important questions nevertheless remain regarding the algorithm's validity with other populations (e.g., non-English speakers) and generalizability to other measurement contexts and geographic regions (e.g. daily social environments in other cultures). Next, while these four samples span three iterations of the EAR (e.g., PocketEAR, iEAR, and Android EAR), the performance of the CAD algorithm will still need to be tested with more recent EAR versions (which now, for example, feature stereo recording) and data collected from other ambient audio sampling methods.

Implications and Conclusions

On the background of current calls to address the social isolation epidemic in the United States (and in other countries), the psychometric validation of an algorithm for the automatic "sensing" of conversation activity from real-world ambient audio responds to the nationwide call for consistent and accurate measurement of social connection (Office of Surgeon General, 2023).

While the CAD algorithm we have validated here is anything but a tool for the measurement of all aspects of social connection, it does provide researchers with a viable way to objectively capture one important slice of it, the degree to which individuals engage in spoken conversations with others. This is important because, so far, researchers have mostly had to rely on prompted momentary self-reports when studying social interactions in everyday life, which are effectively limited to a few assessments per day. The availability of an algorithm to automatically capture conversation activity renders naturalistic observation research with an otherwise highly resourceintensive method such as the EAR more feasible. And it can get us one step closer to the ability to continuously and passively assess social interactions at a granularity with which we routinely continuously and passively assess physical activity. Naturally, researchers may be curious about different interaction types and aspects of interaction quality. Drawing a parallel to wearablebased physical activity assessment, we argue that a simple (one may say simplistic) measure of quantity can go a long way: People routinely track their daily step count and consider it important feedback about their physical activity (irrespective of the "type" or "quality" of a step, say walking or running or doing uphill or downhill). At the same time, we are excited about the recent progress in ambient audio signal processing and what it can mean for researchers' ability to track a broader range of biomarkers of social connection (Hebbar et al., 2024; Virtanen, Plumbley, & Ellis, 2018). For the CAD algorithm, this would mean first moving from the current desktop processing of conversation activity to passive and privacy protective, in-the-moment wearable sensing, similarly to the StudentLife application (Harari et al., 2020) and SocialBit (Dhand et al., 2026). From there, moving towards a validated assessment of features beyond mere quantity (e.g., valence, quality, conversation partner, type of conversation) would be an exciting step as research has found these social interaction features to also clearly matter for psychological and physical well-being (Merolla & Hall, 2025). However, as with the current study, we believe that it will be important to subject any to-be-developed algorithm to a systematic and comprehensive psychometric construct validation so that psychologists can rely on the sensed behaviors as real, in the sense of responsibly usable, psychological measures.

Generative AI was not used in the preparation of this manuscript.

Additionally, the current study focused solely on the CAD algorithm's convergent validity from the perspective of reproducing between-person variability and recovering betweenperson effects. Put more specifically, the current results suggest CAD is valid as a measure of individual differences in conversation tendency. An open question remains regarding the extent to which the CAD algorithm can also accurately reproduce within-person variability and recover within-person effects (Hamaker, 2012). In that regard, preliminary analyses using Sample 4 data aggregated to the daily level suggest that, at the absolute level, the ground-truth codings capture more variance than the CAD algorithm at both the between-person and the within-person level.

At the relative level, which is the level of the intraclass correlation, however, the ratios of between-person to total variance were comparable for the ground-truth codings and the CAD algorithm (yielding a difference in estimates of no more than .031). Further, nearly identical intraclass correlations emerged for CAD VA and for CAD ALL . Given that a potential use case of the CAD algorithm is as a passive sensing measure of social connection trajectories and changes over time (incl. as an intervention target), its systematic validation at the within-person level is an important task for future research. Furthermore, in this paper, we primarily validated the CAD algorithm with respect to its default output, the posterior probabilities that a sound file contains an instance of conversation.

We focused on the validation of the algorithm's original, continuous metric, rather than a metric derived from thresholding, because we believe the posterior probabilities provide maximal robustness (e.g., optimal thresholds can vary by sample features) and potentially greater granularity (e.g., they might carry information about the degree of preponderance of conversation in a sound file). Yet the CAD appeared to be relatively strict (or "stingy") in classifying conversation, as it underestimated conversational activity and captured less
